extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, metaphysics, or philosophy seeking definitions and classification of 'things' (feelings, substances, attributes)
extracted.subtask_description: Provide a logical/metaphysical taxonomy and definitions of what can be named: (1) Feelings, (2) Substances (body and mind), and (3) Attributes (quality, relation, quantity), together with account of how knowledge of them is grounded in states of consciousness (sensations, thoughts, emotions, volitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Namable Things
rubrics_metrics.description: The enumeration of all varieties of Things capable of being named or predicated: (1) Feelings, (2) Substances, and (3) Attributes. (Summary: Feelings first; Substances as Bodies or Minds; Attributes as Quality, Relation, Quantity.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text frames this as the primary organizational rubric for logical inquiry: begin by distinguishing feelings (sensations, thoughts, emotions, volitions), then treat substances (body and mind) and finally analyze attributes under the three heads. The §15 general results summarizes this taxonomy and its consequences for what can be known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feelings taxonomy (sensations, thoughts, emotions, volitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings are of four sorts: Sensations, Thoughts, Emotions, and Volitions; Perceptions are a particular case of Belief; Actions are volitions followed by an effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this four-fold division as the basic category when analyzing mental states. When explaining knowledge or predication, reduce occurrences to these kinds of feelings (e.g., perceptions = belief). The text treats feelings as the primary data of consciousness on which other categories are grounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance: Body defined as unknown external cause (substratum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Body is described as the unknown external cause or substratum to which we refer sensations; all we can know of matter are the sensations it gives us and their order of occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing bodies, treat them as inferred causes of sensations rather than directly known entities. The text notes philosophical skepticism about proving matter extrinsically and endorses treating the belief in matter as intuitive or as a working hypothesis. Use 'body' to mean that mysterious cause, not an independently accessible 'thing in itself.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance: Mind defined as unknown sentient subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Mind is the unknown recipient or percipient of feelings; we know nothing about the inner nature of the thinking principle beyond the series of its states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define mind analogously to body but as the sentient subject. Explanations of mental attributes should be grounded on the series of feelings constituting consciousness; avoid claiming knowledge of any inmost nature beyond states of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes taxonomy: Quality, Relation, Quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes are distributed under three heads—Quality, Quantity, and Relation—and these are grounded on sensations or states of consciousness that objects excite in us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite division to classify predicates applied to things. For logical purposes, treat attributes as linguistic/conceptual labels for certain recurring states of consciousness or capacities to produce them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality defined as grounded on sensations (foundation of quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quality (example: whiteness) is grounded on the sensation which the object excites; two views are acknowledged: (a) quality = the sensation itself, (b) quality = a power in the object that produces the sensation. The text adopts language compatible with either view but insists the sensation is the only part provable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting a quality, show that the corresponding sensation occurs. Be cautious of reifying an occult 'power' beyond the observable regularity. For logical proofs, demonstrate the sensation (foundation) rather than posit hidden qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation defined via fundamentum relationis (joint fact/phenomenon)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation between two things exists when there is some fact or phenomenon (the fundamentum relationis) in which both enter as parties concerned; relations are grounded on such facts or series of facts, which are themselves states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze any alleged relation by identifying the underlying fact/phenomenon that involves both relata. For legal, social, or causal relations, reduce the fundamentum to relevant thoughts, feelings, volitions, or observable acts (i.e., mental states and their effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance, antecedence, succession, simultaneity as sui generis relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Likeness/unlikeness and temporal relations (antecedence, consequence, simultaneity) are special: they are states of consciousness (feelings of resemblance or of succession) and do not admit the same analyzability as other relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these relations as primitive in analysis: they are experienced as feelings (resemblance, succession) and cannot be fully reduced to other facts without leaving the bounds of the logical inquiry. Recognize the ambiguity between identity and indistinguishable resemblance when using 'same'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity grounded on differences in sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences of quantity (e.g., a gallon vs ten gallons) are grounded on differences in the sensations they produce; quantity is the aspect in which two items differ when their sensations partly resemble and partly differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting quantitative differences, relate them to observable differences in the sensations or experiences they produce. Do not posit an independent ontological category of quantity separate from its experiential grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes of minds include their own states and effects on others
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes ascribed to minds are grounded either on the mind's own states (habits of feeling, e.g., devout, cheerful) or on the effects the mind produces in other minds (e.g., admiration excited by a character).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing qualities to persons, separate (a) predicates about their internal habitual states and (b) predicates about the responses they evoke in others. Recognize that value terms (admirable, generous) often combine both aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological conclusion: epistemic limit — we know only sensations and order
rubrics_metrics.description: All we can know of the outward world is the sensations it gives us and the order of their occurrence; likewise, the inner nature of mind is known only via its states of consciousness. Thus logical predication must be founded on these states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a methodological humility in epistemic claims: limit proofs and definitions to what can be grounded in sensation or conscious states. Avoid metaphysical assertions about 'things in themselves' beyond this grounding; when used, treat them as hypothetical or intuitive.
